stem: What are the typical mechanisms for installing a custom or third-party application on a ServiceNow instance?

options.text: The ServiceNow Store, a private app repo, and Update Sets.
Only ServiceNow Support can install apps.
By copy-pasting JavaScript into the console.
By emailing the app's sys_app sys_id to ServiceNow.

rationale: Three common install paths: ServiceNow Store (the marketplace), an internal/private repo (App Manager → company's apps), and Update Set transfers for direct between-instance moves. The right choice depends on audience and how you distribute.

stem: What is the ServiceNow Store?

options.text: A shopping mall in Santa Clara.

rationale: ServiceNow Store is the curated marketplace. Listed apps have passed certification (security, quality, packaging). Customers browse and install through their instance's App Manager.

stem: On the Custom Application record, what does the Version field control?

options.text: The number of users licensed to use the app.

rationale: Version drives install/upgrade decisions. The platform compares incoming-app version with installed version; if newer, it upgrades; if same, it can either skip or reinstall depending on options. Bump it every release so users get upgrades cleanly.

stem: Your custom app depends on the 'Customer Service Management' plugin. A customer tries to install your app on an instance that doesn't have CSM activated. What's the expected behavior, and the right design choice?

options.text: The app installs normally and silently fails at runtime when CSM features are touched.
Declare the dependency on the sys_app record's Dependencies related list.
Email customers asking if they have CSM.
Skip CSM features for those installs without warning the customer.

rationale: Declared dependencies = explicit install-time checks. The platform either activates the dependency or refuses to install with a meaningful message. Silent runtime failure is the worst outcome and exactly what dependency metadata prevents.

distractor_notes.C: Email is no substitute for declarative dependency.
distractor_notes.D: Silently skipping breaks the customer's expectations.

stem: What does 'publish an application' mean in ServiceNow?

options.text: Package the current state of the application.
Email the app to ServiceNow Support.

rationale: Publishing captures the app's current state as a versioned release artifact. The artifact is what target instances install. From there, you bump the source app's version for the next release and start the next cycle.

stem: A developer wants to ship their custom app to a customer's instance, but the customer isn't on the ServiceNow Store and won't be. What is the supported workflow?

options.text: Publish the app to an Update Set.
Hand-build every table on the customer's instance.
Use a USB drive to copy files between instances.

rationale: Publish-to-Update-Set + customer Retrieve/Commit is the off-Store distribution path. Works fine for one-to-one delivery or internal distribution where the Store isn't appropriate.

distractor_notes.C: Hand-building defeats the point of having an app.

stem: A customer wants to uninstall a custom app. They click Uninstall in App Manager. What's true about the result?

options.text: Uninstall is reversible — click Reinstall and the data comes back.
Uninstall has no effect at all.

rationale: Uninstall drops the app's artifacts and any tables they own. The records living in those tables go with them. Plan a data export or migration before uninstalling. (Some apps offer 'soft' uninstalls that leave data — read the app's docs first.)

distractor_notes.D: Anthropic has nothing to do with ServiceNow licensing.

stem: What is App Engine Management Center (AEMC)?

options.text: A console for managing custom apps.
A type of UI Action button.

rationale: AEMC is the org-level app management view — installed apps, where they're deployed, what versions, lifecycle status. Useful when an organization has many custom apps in flight across many instances.

stem: When the platform installs a NEW version of an app on an instance that already has an older version, what happens?

options.text: Nothing — the older version stays, the new install is ignored.
An upgrade applying version differences to existing artifacts.
The platform refuses to install anything.

rationale: Newer-version installs are upgrades. The platform diffs and applies. Data on existing app tables is preserved. (You can also script upgrade-specific logic if data needs to be migrated between schema versions.)

distractor_notes.D: Apps don't run multiple versions side-by-side.

stem: Your company maintains its own private library of internal apps that should NOT appear in the public ServiceNow Store. What is the right distribution mechanism?

options.text: Publish to the company's private app repository.

rationale: Company applications give internal-only distribution. Instances belonging to your organization see them in App Manager; the public Store doesn't list them. The right channel for internal-only apps.

distractor_notes.C: Email distribution isn't a real install workflow.
distractor_notes.D: Internal apps are common and supported.

stem: A developer is using semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). For an internal-only bug fix that doesn't change the schema or add features, which version bump is appropriate?

options.text: Bump PATCH for a bug fix.

rationale: SemVer convention: PATCH for bug fixes, MINOR for backwards-compatible features, MAJOR for breaking. Following the convention makes upgrade decisions easier for downstream consumers.

distractor_notes.A: MAJOR signals breaking changes — overkill for a fix.
distractor_notes.C: Skipping the bump means installs can't tell new from old.
distractor_notes.D: Bumping MAJOR every time turns versions into noise.

stem: A team's release process is: developer commits to update set on Dev → manually transfers to Test → manually transfers to Prod. Releases take 2 days of clicking and frequently miss artifacts. What is the right improvement?
rationale: Mature release pipelines treat the app as an artifact, version it, and move the same artifact through environments. AEMC and platform APIs make this more automatable. Skipping environments or developing in prod is how disasters happen.

distractor_notes.A: More clickers isn't a process improvement.

stem: What is Team Development in ServiceNow?
rationale: Team Development is the platform's built-in source-control-style collaboration tool. Multiple dev instances coordinate via a parent instance; developers push/pull changes, compare versions, and review.

stem: In Team Development, what does the platform use to back its versioning system?

options.text: A flat file in the filesystem.

rationale: Team Development is platform-native versioning (not Git). The platform separately offers Git integration for source-control-style workflows that DO use Git. Don't confuse the two — they solve related but different problems. (A common CAD exam trick.)

distractor_notes.A: Team Development is NOT Git-backed. Git is a separate, complementary integration.

stem: Five developers are working on the same app across five development instances. Team Development is configured. Developer A wants to publish her finished changes so Developer B can pull them. What is the workflow?

options.text: Developer A emails her Update Set XML to Developer B.
Developer A asks an admin to copy records by hand.
Both developers stop working until Friday.

rationale: Parent-child push/pull is the Team Development model. The parent is the shared baseline. Devs push their work up, pull peers' work down. Conflicts get resolved via the version-comparison UI.

stem: What is the central instance in a Team Development setup typically called?
rationale: Parent and child are the canonical Team Development terms. The parent is the shared origin; children are developer working instances.

distractor_notes.A: Production isn't typically the Team Development parent.

stem: What does ServiceNow's Git integration enable for app developers?

options.text: ServiceNow ships a free Git client.
Git is required for all Team Development setups.

rationale: ServiceNow Git integration links an application to a real Git repo (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket). Records are serialized to files, you branch/merge/review off-platform, and apply changes back. Useful for engineering teams that want their full SDLC stack.

distractor_notes.D: Team Development and Git are independent options.

stem: A team is choosing between Team Development and the Git integration. Team Development is integrated with ServiceNow records natively; Git allows external code review tools and branching workflows. Which is the right choice?
rationale: Team Development is the on-platform answer; Git is the bring-your-engineering-SDLC answer. Use whichever fits the team. The trap is doctrinal certainty — there's no universal best.

stem: A team wants peer review on every change before it goes to test. With Team Development, what's the natural way to do this?

options.text: Compare pushed changes in Team Development.
Use Microsoft Word to compare scripts.

rationale: Team Development supports record-level diff, comparison, and review workflows. Reviewers see exactly what changed and gate the promotion. That's the platform-native code review story.

distractor_notes.B: Wishful thinking isn't a review process.
distractor_notes.D: Word isn't a review tool for the platform.

stem: Which is true about Update Sets and applications?

options.text: Any developer change is captured in an Update Set.
Update Sets only apply to apps from the ServiceNow Store.
Update Sets only apply to UI Policies.

rationale: Update Sets capture customizations everywhere. They're foundational regardless of whether you're using Team Development or Git on top. New developers sometimes try to skip Update Sets and discover, late, that their changes are stuck on Dev.

distractor_notes.B: Update Sets apply to all customizations.

stem: Two developers on different instances both edit the same Business Rule. They both push to parent. What happens?

options.text: The second push is silently discarded.

rationale: Concurrent changes to the same record = conflict. The platform surfaces it for resolution rather than silently overwriting. That's how any version-control system has to behave — and how to teach teams to coordinate.

distractor_notes.A: Silent loss would be worse than a conflict.
distractor_notes.D: One Business Rule record can't be two versions.

stem: Which best describes branching in ServiceNow's Git integration?

options.text: An app linked to Git can be developed on a branch.
Branching is automatic and can't be controlled.

rationale: Git-style branching belongs to the Git integration path. The team works on branches in the connected repo, and instance state follows whichever branch is chosen. Team Development on its own doesn't model Git branches.

stem: Where do developers typically see a unified view of Team Development activity — pushes, pulls, conflicts, comparisons?
rationale: The Team Development Dashboard is the feature's hub — recent pushes/pulls, pending conflicts, comparison entry points. Bookmark it if you're using Team Development.

stem: A team has 6 developers, 6 dev instances, no Team Development, no Git, and a folder of XML Update Sets they email each other. Releases are chaotic. What is the most impactful next step?
rationale: Email-shuffled Update Sets is the failure mode the platform solves with Team Development or Git. Adopt a shared origin and the rest of the chaos calms down. Hiring or stopping work doesn't address the underlying problem.

distractor_notes.A: More devs would multiply the chaos.
distractor_notes.C: Email isn't the right channel for code distribution.
distractor_notes.D: Stopping is not a process improvement.

stem: What is a 'customer update' in ServiceNow's parlance?

options.text: A record change from a customization.
A purchase made by a customer.

rationale: Customer updates are tracked customizations — Business Rules, scripts, dictionary changes, etc. — captured as sys_update_xml records. They are the units that Update Sets carry between instances.

stem: On committing an Update Set, the Preview reports several 'skipped' records: incoming changes that the platform refused to apply because the target instance already has a newer or conflicting version. What's the right next step?
rationale: Skipped records are calls for human judgment. The platform won't decide between conflicting versions — you have to. Spend time here rather than rushing the commit.

distractor_notes.C: Deleting the set throws away the work.

stem: When changes are made inside a custom application scope, where are they typically captured?

options.text: The Default Update Set of the Global scope.
A 'Default' Update Set for that application scope.

rationale: Each application scope has its own current Update Set context. New scope-changes land in that scope's Default unless the developer has selected a different Update Set in the scope. This is why 'I switched scope and now my changes are missing' panic happens — they're in the scope's Default.

distractor_notes.C: Scope changes absolutely transport via Update Sets.

stem: What is Instance Scan in ServiceNow?
rationale: Instance Scan is the platform's automated quality auditor. It evaluates code, configuration, and platform usage against built-in (and customer-defined) check rules. Use it before releases to catch known anti-patterns and tech debt.

stem: What is the Automated Test Framework (ATF) in ServiceNow?
rationale: ATF is ServiceNow's built-in test harness. Author tests in the platform, run them on demand, integrate with release workflows. Great for regression testing custom apps — and ServiceNow strongly recommends running ATF suites before upgrading versions.

stem: A team is upgrading their instance to a new ServiceNow release. They have 40 custom apps. What is the recommended quality gate for the upgrade?

options.text: Click Upgrade and hope nothing breaks.
Email all users to test by hand.
Disable all custom apps before upgrade.

rationale: ATF + clone-of-prod is the responsible upgrade gate. Catch regressions on the clone, fix them, then upgrade the real instance with confidence. Disabling apps to skip testing means you didn't actually upgrade safely.

distractor_notes.C: User-driven manual testing at scale doesn't work.

stem: Which is a typical multi-instance environment topology for a ServiceNow customer?
rationale: Dev → Test → Prod is the canonical topology, sometimes with extras (UAT, staging, training, sandbox). Each environment has its purpose; promotions flow through them with gates so prod never sees untested code.

distractor_notes.C: Prod-only means there's nowhere safe to break things.
distractor_notes.D: Customers don't run ServiceNow on laptops.

stem: A developer commits an Update Set on Test with no preview errors, but on Prod the same Update Set throws an error about a missing referenced table. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The referenced table existed on Test.

rationale: Environment drift is the silent killer of 'works on my machine' — Test had something Prod doesn't. Either include the prerequisite in the set, deploy the prerequisite first, or check the source environment for dependencies you forgot to track.

distractor_notes.B: Don't blame the environment as the first hypothesis.

stem: A developer wants to delete their custom app from the dev instance cleanly. What is the right path?
rationale: Use the supported Delete Application workflow. It handles the dependency-graph correctly. Hand-deleting sys_app leaves orphans (the artifacts, the customer updates) and creates exactly the kind of mess that makes future deploys painful.

distractor_notes.C: Customers don't drop the platform database.
distractor_notes.D: Stopping use doesn't reclaim resources or clean up.

stem: A team gets a quality complaint: their app is buggy after every release. They want to ship more confidently. What is the most impactful single improvement?

options.text: Hire a contractor to test the app once at the end of the year.
Build ATF tests for critical journeys, run on each promote.

rationale: Automated tests + promotion gates is THE quality lever. One-shot manual testing doesn't scale. ATF is the platform's built-in test framework — use it.

distractor_notes.A: Annual contractor testing is too sparse.
distractor_notes.C: Stopping new features doesn't fix the release quality problem.
distractor_notes.D: Asking users to expect bugs is the wrong response.

stem: Why is it considered a best practice to keep Update Sets small and focused (one feature or bug fix per set), rather than letting one giant set accumulate weeks of unrelated changes?

options.text: There's no benefit — bigger is fine.
Small sets ease review and revert.
Smaller sets take longer to commit.

rationale: Small, focused sets are an engineering hygiene best practice — easier to review, easier to revert, lower blast radius. Treat each Update Set like a pull request: a clear, scoped, mergeable change.

stem: Looking at the full lifecycle of a custom ServiceNow application, which sequence reflects mature engineering practice?

options.text: Plan → design data model → develop on Dev with Update Sets.
Build directly in Prod, no testing, no version.
Develop the entire app on a USB drive, then plug it into Prod.
Skip data model design and figure it out later.

rationale: That's the responsible lifecycle in compressed form: deliberate design, source control, testing, gated promotion, monitoring. Every shortcut from this list eventually gets paid back — usually with interest, in production.

distractor_notes.B: Prod-only development is the path to disaster.
distractor_notes.C: USB-drive deployment isn't a ServiceNow workflow.
